papers.citation: Motoki Osada, Bai Yang Wang, Berit H. Goodge, Kyuho Lee, Hyeok Yoon, Keita Sakuma, Danfeng Li, Masashi Miura, Lena F. Kourkoutis, and Harold Y. Hwang, “A Superconducting Praseodymium Nickelate with Infinite Layer Structure,” Nano Letters 2020, 20(8), 5735–5740.
papers.equations_or_assumptions: No spatial-percolation equation, Hamiltonian, or one-orbital model is developed. The operational definitions reported are Tc,onset as the temperature where resistivity is 90% of its value at 20 K, Tc,zero as the zero-resistance temperature, and Jc(T) estimated from the maximum in dV/dI. The paper interprets the mutual-inductance response below Tc,zero as diamagnetic screening and global superconductivity. Its rare-earth comparison motivates an inference about necessary 4f effects; it does not isolate or directly measure a microscopic pairing mechanism.
papers.evidence_stance: Verified as an exact journal paper. The full accessible primary manuscript supports the described synthesis, measurement methods, results, operational definitions, and stated caveats. Treat the proposed insensitivity to rare-earth 4f details as the authors’ interpretation from a Pr–Nd comparison, not as proof of mechanism. Supplementary-information status is unresolved, not evidence that no supplement exists.

papers.limitations: This is a thin-film materials synthesis and characterization report centered on one Sr concentration (x=0.2), not a comprehensive Pr phase diagram or a microscopic mechanism study. The authors state they had not yet performed an equally extensive optimization study for Pr films and explicitly say the role of 4f magnetism is unknown. Across the five films tested, Tc and normal-state resistivity did not vary systematically with thickness, but normal-state resistivity showed sample-to-sample variability attributed by the authors to extended defects. The evidence supports superconductivity in the measured films but does not identify its pairing mechanism or establish that every infinite-layer nickelate shares identical behavior.
papers.main_findings: The paper reports successful synthesis of infinite-layer PrNiO2 and Pr0.8Sr0.2NiO2 films. The doped films show a superconducting transition with onset Tc=12 K and zero-resistance Tc=7 K, and a critical current density of 334 kA/cm² at 2 K. Mutual-inductance data show a diamagnetic screening response below the zero-resistance transition, interpreted as global superconductivity; the inferred London penetration depth is on the micron scale. The undoped PrNiO2 film has a low-temperature resistivity upturn. The authors argue that comparable superconductivity in Pr- and Nd-based films makes finely tuned rare-earth 4f hybridization and Nd-specific valence fluctuations unnecessary, while the role of 4f magnetism remains unknown.
papers.methods_and_model: Experimental thin-film study, not a theoretical or tight-binding modeling paper. PrNiO3 and Pr0.8Sr0.2NiO3 precursor films were grown by pulsed-laser deposition on SrTiO3(001), then topotactically reduced with CaH2 to PrNiO2 and Pr0.8Sr0.2NiO2. Characterization included X-ray diffraction and reciprocal-space mapping, cross-sectional STEM/EELS, four-probe resistivity, patterned-device current–voltage measurements, and two-coil mutual-inductance measurements. The authors examined five doped films 5.3–12 nm thick, including one with a 2 nm SrTiO3 cap.
papers.relationship_to_projects: Spatial percolation manuscript: relevant experimental context for superconducting Pr0.8Sr0.2NiO2 films, film thicknesses, extended-defect variability, and the need to distinguish zero resistance from bulk/global screening. It does not model spatial inhomogeneity, connectivity, percolation thresholds, or local superconducting domains, so it is not direct validation of a percolation model. One-orbital interface tight-binding notebook: relevant as a material/platform reference for epitaxial Pr-based infinite-layer films on SrTiO3, square-planar NiO2 structure, strain, and an observed superconducting state. It does not provide an interface tight-binding Hamiltonian, orbital-resolved bands, fitted hopping parameters, or a one-orbital justification; any mapping to that notebook would require independent theoretical or spectroscopic support.
papers.research_question: Can Pr-based infinite-layer nickelate films be synthesized, and does Sr-doped Pr0.8Sr0.2NiO2 superconduct? The authors also use Pr as a comparison with Nd to test whether superconductivity requires specific rare-earth 4f electronic effects, including direct 4f hybridization or Nd valence fluctuations.

papers.equations_or_assumptions: The composition is parameterized as La1−xCaxNiO2, with Ca2+ substitution for La3+ treated as hole doping. The phase diagram’s onset temperature is operationally defined by a resistivity drop to 90% of the normal-state value (the figure caption specifies the 10 K reference value). The upper-critical-field analysis uses a Ginzburg–Landau fit and yields an in-plane zero-temperature coherence length of 4.59 nm for the representative film. No proposed spatial-percolation equation or one-orbital interface Hamiltonian is developed in this paper. The authors discuss Hall-sign changes as suggestive of multiband/electronic-structure changes, not as a unique direct measurement of a band count or mechanism.

papers.full_text_status: The publisher’s DOI record and the complete primary article text in PubMed Central were accessible and inspected; this was not an abstract-only verification. S1–S6, but attempts to retrieve the PDF were blocked by a PMC browser-verification/reCAPTCHA page, so the supplement itself was not inspected.
papers.limitations: The article does not provide a dedicated limitations section. Its evidence is from Ca-doped LaNiO2 thin films over the tested composition range, and the reported results do not by themselves establish a microscopic pairing mechanism or spatially resolved superconducting connectivity. The authors explicitly call for further theoretical and experimental work to clarify the role of 4f orbitals in the (multi)band nature of nickelates and the distinctive Hall-sign-change behavior. The supplementary PDF is available by link in the article record but was inaccessible during this verification, so supplementary-only details were not checked.
papers.main_findings: The reported phase diagram has a superconducting dome over approximately 0.15 < x < 0.3. Undoped and underdoped samples through x≤0.15 are insulating from 300 K down to 2 K; the overdoped x≥0.3 samples show increased normal-state resistivity and weakly insulating low-temperature behavior. For higher doping, the Hall coefficient changes sign on cooling in most reported samples at x≥0.23 (the paper notes an exception at x=0.25); the sign-change temperature is around 35 K and does not appreciably shift with doping in that regime. A representative x=0.23 film was reported as 17 nm thick and showed an infinite-layer structure by STEM. The authors interpret the data as evidence that lattice environment/dopant identity and multiband structure matter, while treating the detailed mechanism as unresolved.
papers.methods_and_model: The authors made nominal La1−xCaxNiO3 perovskite precursor films by pulsed-laser deposition on TiO2-terminated (001) SrTiO3, then used CaH2 topotactic reduction to obtain the infinite-layer films. They characterized structure using synchrotron X-ray diffraction and cross-sectional HAADF-STEM, and measured resistivity and Hall transport in a physical-property measurement system. For x=0.23, field suppression of superconductivity was analyzed by fitting upper-critical-field versus midpoint-transition data with a Ginzburg–Landau model. The study is an experimental film/transport investigation, not a microscopic tight-binding or spatial-percolation model.
papers.relationship_to_projects: For the spatial percolation manuscript, the paper is useful as an experimental benchmark for a doping-dependent superconducting dome and insulating transport regimes in an infinite-layer nickelate, but it does not measure spatial superconducting patches, connectivity, or a percolation threshold; it cannot directly validate a percolation model. For the one-orbital interface tight-binding notebook, it offers qualitative empirical context for doping-dependent transport and the influence of lattice environment, but it contains no interface-specific tight-binding calculation and no one-orbital model. Its discussion of multiband structure and lattice/dopant effects is a caution against presenting a one-orbital model as a complete description of this material without independent justification.
papers.research_question: Whether Ca substitution in infinite-layer La1−xCaxNiO2 thin films can produce superconductivity, and how the superconducting phase diagram and normal-state transport (particularly the Hall coefficient) evolve with Ca content, in relation to the electronic and lattice behavior of other infinite-layer nickelates.

papers.citation: A. S. Botana and M. R. Norman, "Similarities and Differences between LaNiO2 and CaCuO2 and Implications for Superconductivity," Physical Review X 10, 011024 (2020).
papers.equations_or_assumptions: The charge-transfer energy is defined as Δ = ε_d − ε_p. The single-band fit is written ε(k) = Σ_i t_i f_i(k), with six fitted terms and interlayer form factors; the paper defines t′/t = (|t_3| + |t_2|)/|t_1|, obtaining 0.37 in each material. Orbital-energy centroids are calculated as E_i = ∫g_i(E)E dE / ∫g_i(E), with integration over the antibonding eg band complex. A rigid-band approximation is used for one estimate of effective doping and optimal doping. The authors also use chosen Wannier projections (five transition-metal d and six oxygen p orbitals, with spacer-cation d_z2 inclusion improving fits); they explicitly describe the Wannier transformation as faithful but not unique.
papers.evidence_stance: The candidate is verified as an exact published citation: title, authors, journal, volume/article number, publication year, and DOI agree across the APS DOI/publisher record and independent institutional/arXiv records. The accessible arXiv v3 provides full-paper evidence for the reported methods and findings. The APS supplement is confirmed to exist and its declared scope is known, but the supplemental file itself was not inspected; no supplement-only claim is used.
papers.full_text_status: The APS publisher record and DOI were consulted, and a complete readable arXiv manuscript (v3, arXiv:1908.10946) was accessible. APS lists supplemental material covering band structures, Fermi surfaces, Wannier functions, Slater-Koster fits, Hall calculations, and magnetic band structures. The supplement landing/description was inspected, but the supplemental file itself could not be retrieved because APS access returned a Cloudflare challenge; supplement-specific findings therefore are not claimed here.
papers.limitations: This is a computational comparative electronic-structure study, not a direct experimental test of superconductivity or a derivation of a superconducting order parameter. Results depend on the chosen DFT and LDA+U treatments, crystal structures, Wannier projections, and fitting assumptions. The rigid-band doping estimate is an approximation; the paper separately uses finite Sr-doped supercells. LaNiO2 is emphasized to avoid complications from Nd 4f states, so detailed Nd-specific f-electron physics is outside the central comparison. The authors report that their magnetic calculations yield C-type AFM even though experimental AFM order was not established, highlighting uncertainty in interpreting that prediction. The manuscript has no dedicated limitations section. The supplemental file's detailed results were not available for independent inspection in this verification.
papers.main_findings: The calculated one-band fits give t′/t = 0.37 for both LaNiO2 and CaCuO2, with nickelate nearest-neighbor hopping magnitude about 80% of the cuprate value. Wannier-derived d-p charge-transfer energy is substantially larger for LaNiO2 (4.4 eV) than CaCuO2 (2.7 eV), while the Wannier eg splitting is comparable (0.7 versus 1.0 eV). Rare-earth 5d electron pockets near the Fermi level self-dope the nickelate's large hole-like d_x2-y2 Fermi surface; the calculations find that Sr doping suppresses rare-earth-derived states and makes the electronic structure more single-band/cuprate-like. GGA spin-polarized calculations find a C-type antiferromagnetic solution for LaNiO2, but the paper notes the lack of experimental evidence for antiferromagnetic order. The authors conclude that several cuprate-associated electronic parameters are favorable, while the larger charge-transfer energy and rare-earth pockets remain important differences; these are electronic-structure implications, not a demonstrated superconducting mechanism.
papers.methods_and_model: First-principles calculations used the all-electron WIEN2k APW+lo method. Nonmagnetic calculations used PBE-GGA; Ni correlations were also examined with LDA+U in fully localized limit and around-mean-field schemes (U_Ni = 1.4–6 eV, J = 0.8 eV). They compared LaNiO2 with CaCuO2 and noted that NdNiO2's band structure is nearly identical to LaNiO2's for their purpose. Maximally localized Wannier functions and Slater-Koster fits supplied orbital and hopping parameters. A six-parameter single-band tight-binding fit described the Fermi-level d_x2-y2 antibonding band. Magnetic configurations and Sr-doped supercells were also studied; Hall coefficients were calculated from the band structure. Lattice parameters, k-point mesh, convergence settings, and supercell sizes are specified in the manuscript.
papers.relationship_to_projects: For the spatial percolation manuscript, this paper is contextual materials/electronic-structure background only. It does not formulate spatial percolation, connectivity thresholds, disorder-driven cluster formation, or transport through percolating paths, so it is not evidence for a percolation claim. For the one-orbital interface tight-binding notebook, it is more directly useful as a parameterization reference: it provides a d_x2-y2-derived single-band fit and reports t′/t = 0.37 for both comparison materials, alongside multiorbital Wannier parameters. However, it does not model interfaces or spatially varying interface hoppings, and its fitted parameters should not be assumed to apply to the notebook's interface geometry without separate justification. Its multiorbital comparison also cautions that reducing the nickelate to one orbital leaves out rare-earth pockets and the larger d-p splitting.
papers.research_question: What electronic-structure and magnetic similarities and differences distinguish infinite-layer RNiO2 (R = La, Nd) from the cuprate CaCuO2, and what do those comparisons imply for nickelate superconductivity? The authors focus on hopping amplitudes, orbital energy splittings, charge-transfer energy, spacer-cation states, magnetism, and the evolution under Sr doping.

papers.citation: Yusuke Nomura, Motoaki Hirayama, Terumasa Tadano, Yoshihide Yoshimoto, Kazuma Nakamura, and Ryotaro Arita, “Formation of a two-dimensional single-component correlated electron system and band engineering in the nickelate superconductor NdNiO2,” Physical Review B 100, 205138 (2019), published 26 November 2019.
papers.equations_or_assumptions: The manuscript defines mode-resolved electron-phonon coupling as lambda_(q,nu)=2/[N(E_F) N_k omega_(q,nu)] times the sum over m,n,k of |g_(mn,nu)(k,q)|^2 delta(xi_(m,q)) delta(xi_(n,k+q)); alpha^2F(omega)=(1/(2N_q)) sum_(q,nu) lambda_(q,nu) omega_(q,nu) delta(omega−omega_(q,nu)); and lambda=2 integral_0^infinity alpha^2F(omega)/omega d omega. The Allen-Dynes Tc estimates use mu*=0.1. The downfolded low-energy description is a Wannier tight-binding model with cRPA interactions; the single-orbital parameters reported are U=2.608 eV, t=−0.370 eV, t'=0.092 eV, and t''=−0.045 eV in the Quantum ESPRESSO parameterization. cRPA excludes screening processes internal to the chosen active subspace, so U depends on which orbitals are retained. Nd 4f states are treated as frozen core in the described calculations. The bulk electronic model uses experimental NdNiO2 lattice parameters; the phonon calculations use separately optimized lattice parameters. Proposed compounds and pocket suppression are computational predictions, not reported synthesis or measurement results.
papers.evidence_stance: Exact candidate exists and the supplied authors, publication year, venue, article number, and DOI are confirmed. The APS publisher metadata and Crossref record establish the published citation; arXiv supplies the accessible full manuscript. Bibliographic verification is high confidence. Technical claims are attributed to the arXiv v2 manuscript and are theoretical calculations/predictions rather than independent experimental verification. No separate supplemental file was located through the APS supplemental endpoint or the arXiv record; the accessible appendices are part of the manuscript. papers.limitations: The paper is a first-principles/modeling study, not a spatial-disorder or percolation analysis, and it does not calculate a superconducting pairing state or establish the mechanism of the observed superconductivity. Its phonon result tests the conventional electron-phonon channel as an exclusive explanation under the stated calculation and Allen-Dynes assumptions. The effective interactions depend on the Wannier subspace and cRPA screening partition. Nd 4f electrons are frozen in core for the stated calculations. NaNd2NiO4 and NaCa2NiO3 are proposed computational candidates; their predicted band structures do not by themselves establish experimental synthesis or superconductivity. These are limitations of scope/modeling evident from the manuscript, not a list explicitly labeled by the authors as a formal limitations section.
papers.main_findings: The three-orbital Wannier model reproduces the near-Fermi-level bands; Ni-Nd-layer hybridization is reported as very small, and the Ni 3d(x2−y2) band is highly two-dimensional. The Nd-derived pockets occur around Γ and A, and their finite occupation leaves the Ni orbital at about 0.87 filling in the calculation. In cRPA, the Ni onsite U is about 3.1 eV in the three-orbital model and about 2.6 eV in the single-orbital model including Nd-layer screening, a reduction below 20%; the single-band nearest hopping is about −0.37 eV, giving |U/t| about 7. The calculated electron-phonon coupling is lambda=0.22 at the listed 0.04-Ry smearing and remains below 0.5 for the reported reasonable smearing widths; Allen-Dynes estimates are far below the experimental 9–15 K range, so the paper rules out phonons as the exclusive explanation, not all possible superconducting mechanisms. The authors predict that reducing interstitial-s–cation-dxy hybridization shrinks the extra pockets; these nearly disappear in calculated NaNd2NiO4 and NaCa2NiO3 band structures.
papers.methods_and_model: First-principles electronic structures were calculated with PBE density-functional theory (Quantum ESPRESSO; an xTAPP comparison was also used) and fitted with maximally localized Wannier functions using RESPACK. The minimal model retains Ni 3d(x2−y2), Nd 5d(3z2−r2), and an interstitial-s-centered orbital that bonds with Nd 5dxy. cRPA was used to estimate screened Coulomb parameters for three-orbital and single-orbital subspaces. Phonons and electron-phonon coupling were calculated using density-functional perturbation theory and assessed with the Allen-Dynes formula. For proposed band-engineered compounds, the authors used structural optimization and DFT band calculations. The article also compares an alternative three-orbital representation using Nd 5dxy, and its appendices analyze screening and that alternative model.
papers.relationship_to_projects: For the spatial percolation manuscript, this is background on bulk NdNiO2's multiband electronic structure and screening, not evidence for geometric percolation, spatial connectivity, disorder-driven transitions, or percolation thresholds; do not cite it as support for those results. For the one-orbital interface tight-binding notebook, it provides a useful bulk Ni 3d(x2−y2) reference and one set of hopping/interacting-model parameters, and supports treating Ni-derived states as weakly coupled to Nd-layer bands in this specific bulk calculation. It is not an interface Hamiltonian: it does not derive interface potentials, interfacial hopping, altered coordination, disorder, or layer-dependent parameters. Its single-orbital reduction is a controlled low-energy representation alongside additional Nd-derived pockets, not proof that every interface system is intrinsically single-band.
papers.research_question: The paper asks how Nd-layer states affect the correlated Ni 3d(x2−y2) electrons in parent infinite-layer NdNiO2: what minimal low-energy orbital model captures the Fermi pockets; how strongly Ni and Nd-layer bands hybridize; whether metallic screening from the Nd layer weakens the Ni Hubbard interaction enough to matter for phonon-mediated superconductivity; and whether band engineering can suppress the extra Nd-layer pockets to approach a single-component Mott-Hubbard system.

papers.citation: K.-W. Lee and W. E. Pickett, “Infinite-layer LaNiO₂: Ni¹⁺ is not Cu²⁺,” Physical Review B 70, 165109 (2004).
papers.equations_or_assumptions: For the Ni 3d(x²−y²) band the paper gives εₖ = ε₀ − Σ_R t_R exp(i k·R), with ε₀ = 93 meV, t(100) = 381 meV, t(110) = −81 meV, t(001) = 58 meV, t(111) = −14 meV, and no (101) hopping. This is a fit to a Wannier-like x²−y² band, not a complete model of all states at the Fermi level. The calculations assume the reported majority infinite-layer crystal structure and use LDA or mean-field LDA+U; formal d⁹ valence is discussed as an ionic reference, while the authors caution that a charge-state label has reduced significance in a metal.
papers.evidence_stance: Verified with high confidence: the APS publisher record and independent Crossref metadata agree on the paper’s authorship, Physical Review B volume 70, article 165109, 2004 publication, and DOI; the accessible arXiv manuscript confirms the study’s content. Findings above distinguish the paper’s calculated results from its cited experimental context and explicitly preserve its caveats. The publisher’s full article text was not accessible in this session, but the full arXiv manuscript was.
papers.full_text_status: The APS publisher record and abstract were accessible, but the article body was behind an authorization prompt. The complete 7-page arXiv v1 manuscript (with 8 figures) was accessible and inspected at https://arxiv.org/pdf/cond-mat/0405570. No supplement was listed on the APS record or arXiv record consulted; none was found.
papers.limitations: The work is a band-theory study of the majority infinite-layer phase, not a treatment of the minority disordered phase, synthesis stability, or energetics; the authors explicitly say they do not address stability energetics. Its LDA AFM prediction conflicts with the experimental lack of observed long-range order, and the authors suggest magnetic fluctuations may correct LDA’s magnetic tendency, but do not calculate those fluctuations. The unusual large-U state is explicitly beyond the plausible U range and is sensitive to multiple LDA+U solutions; the paper notes a different U = 8 eV result in earlier work and says the reason for the discrepancy was unknown. The single-band fit does not represent the additional La/Ni-derived Fermi-surface pockets or all orbital mixing.
papers.main_findings: The authors attribute LaNiO₂’s differences from CaCuO₂ mainly to weaker Ni 3d–O 2p mixing, associated with a larger separation of their site energies (at least 2 eV greater than the cuprate comparison), and to low-lying La 5d states mixing with Ni 3d(3z²−r²). The latter produces an additional Fermi-surface pocket and hole-dopes the Ni-derived bands; the calculated Fermi surface is not a single-band surface. LDA yields a weak AFM solution with 0.53 μB per Ni, 6 meV/Ni below the paramagnetic state, despite the cited absence of observed long-range magnetic order. In LDA+U the moment peaks near 0.8 μB at U = 3 eV and declines at larger U; at U = 8 eV, opposing polarization of the x²−y² and 3z²−r² orbitals nearly cancels the net moment. The authors explicitly characterize this large-U state as outside the plausible physical range for LaNiO₂ and not an explanation of its observed behavior.

papers.citation: Massimiliano Stengel and David Vanderbilt, “Berry-phase theory of polar discontinuities at oxide-oxide interfaces,” Physical Review B 80, 241103(R) (2009), published 8 December 2009. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.80.241103.
papers.equations_or_assumptions: In the paper's Gaussian-unit convention, the boundary condition is (D1−D2)·n=0 and D=E+4πP. The interface theorem gives σ_bound=P1−P2; combining this with 4πσ_bound=−E1+E2 yields D1−D2=0. Formal polarization is P=[Σα Qα xα−eΣi xi]/Ω, with ionic cores α and Wannier centers i, and is multivalued modulo e/S (S is interface-cell area). The derivation considers a coherent insulating interface with common in-plane lattice periodicity and a neutral grouping of the interfacial region. The paper notes that its local-polarization construction requires in-plane periodicity; its interface discussion assumes materials thick enough for local distortions to heal and thin enough to avoid dielectric breakdown. The numerical example uses a particular cell/basis grouping; the authors note that more sophisticated cell-volume choices change local Pj by a few percent.
papers.evidence_stance: Verified. The exact title, both authors, Physical Review B volume/article number and Rapid Communication marker, publication year/date, and DOI agree between the APS publisher record and Crossref; the arXiv record independently links the same journal reference and DOI. The complete four-page primary-paper manuscript (arXiv v1, with HTML/PDF) was accessible and read at arXiv/ar5iv. No separate supplement was listed on the APS or arXiv pages inspected.
papers.limitations: The theoretical boundary result is scoped to coherent insulating interfaces and the stated periodicity/neutrality construction; it is not a treatment of conducting interfaces, free-carrier screening, disordered or nonperiodic percolation networks, or arbitrary reconstruction. The worked calculation is a specific idealized 1×1 tetragonal LAO/STO superlattice within LDA, not a general empirical test across oxide interfaces. Polarization is branch-valued and local-cell assignments depend on basis/grouping, so formal and effective local polarization should not be conflated. The paper itself flags that nonperiodic in-plane situations, such as randomly distributed δ-doping, may call for compositional-charge treatment instead. No separate supplement was found/listed in the publisher or arXiv records inspected.
papers.main_findings: For the stated coherent insulating interface, the longitudinal component of D is continuous when P is the formal, branch-valued polarization of the modern theory. The interface bound charge equals the discontinuity in the formal bulk polarizations; the apparent conflict with D continuity arises from treating the polar discontinuity as if it were outside that formal polarization accounting. In the LAO/STO example, the formal local polarization is nearly uniform around the supercell average (reported as −0.365 C/m²), while the effective local polarization pattern has an abrupt jump; the LAO and STO structural distortions point oppositely. Interior layer bucklings agree with constrained-D bulk values to within about 3 mÅ. The relaxed superlattice remains insulating, with a reported gap of about 1.5 eV.
papers.methods_and_model: The authors derive the result using the modern Berry-phase theory of polarization and the interface theorem, defining formal polarization from ionic-core charges and Wannier centers. They also define planar/macroscopically averaged local polarization and displacement. As a first-principles illustration they calculate a periodic tetragonal (LaAlO3)4/(SrTiO3)4, 1×1 superlattice using LDA density-functional theory and PAW, a 60-Ry plane-wave cutoff, a 6×6×1 k-point grid, and relaxed ionic positions and out-of-plane stress. They compare Wannier-based local formal polarization with a Born-effective-charge/displacement estimate of effective polarization, and compare the interior layer relaxations with bulk LAO and STO calculated at the superlattice's constrained D.
papers.relationship_to_projects: Spatial percolation manuscript: relevant as conceptual electrostatic background for how formal polarization discontinuities and normal-D boundary conditions operate across ideal insulating interfaces. It does not derive percolation connectivity, thresholds, cluster statistics, or electrostatics in a spatially disordered/percolating medium, so it cannot by itself validate those manuscript claims. One-orbital interface tight-binding notebook: relevant as motivation for an interface charge/boundary-potential convention and for distinguishing formal interface charge from mobile carriers. The Berry-phase formal polarization and ionic/Wannier charge bookkeeping are not automatically represented by a one-orbital Hamiltonian; a notebook would need explicit background/interface charge and an electrostatic boundary prescription to model analogous effects. The paper does not provide or validate that tight-binding model.
papers.research_question: How should the polar discontinuity and interface charge at a coherent, insulating, charge-mismatched oxide interface be reconciled with the electrostatic boundary condition that the normal component of electric displacement D is continuous? The paper asks whether the usual boundary law can be retained microscopically without introducing a separate compositional-charge term.

papers.citation: Johannes Zierenberg, Niklas Fricke, Martin Marenz, F. P. Spitzner, Viktoria Blavatska, and Wolfhard Janke, "Percolation thresholds and fractal dimensions for square and cubic lattices with long-range correlated defects," Physical Review E 96, 062125 (2017), published 18 December 2017.
papers.equations_or_assumptions: The target long-range covariance decays as C(r)~|r|^(-a), implemented as C(r)=(1+r²)^(-a/2) (or with Manhattan distance). The discrete Fourier spectral density S_k is used to generate Gaussian Fourier components with amplitude proportional to sqrt(S_k), followed by an inverse DFT. Negative S_k values are set to zero (zero-cutoff), which slightly modifies finite-lattice correlations. For unit-variance Gaussian variables, the global occupation probability is p(θ)=1/2 erfc(θ/√2), with a site occupied when τ_x≥θ. The extended Harris scaling assumption is ν_a=2/a for a<a_H=2/ν and ν_a=ν otherwise; the 2D threshold extrapolation uses |p_c−p_c^L|~L^(-1/ν_a), while the 3D fits require correction terms. Fractal dimension is defined through mean largest-cluster mass ⟨V⟩~L^(d_f). These conclusions apply to the specified lattice, correlation construction, mapping, and wrapping criterion.

papers.limitations: The authors explicitly emphasize that p_c is nonuniversal and quantitatively dependent on short-range model details, including the metric and correlation-generation implementation. Their finite-size scaling ansatz for 3D thresholds is empirically motivated; strong correlations produce non-self-averaging/segregation effects, and the a=0.5 and 1 threshold estimates warrant caution. The 3D fractal-dimension fits do not work convincingly for a≤1, and the authors attribute some apparent behavior near the Harris crossover to unmodeled corrections to scaling. Their results are for lattice site percolation, not a general continuum, bond-percolation, or electronic-transport model.
papers.main_findings: Percolation thresholds depend strongly on details of the correlation function and metric, whereas the largest-cluster fractal dimension is reported to be metric-independent within their numerical precision. Correlations generally lower the threshold. Examples from their tables: in 2D at a=0.5, p_c=0.5239(3) for Euclidean distance and 0.5054(3) for Manhattan distance; in 3D at a=0.5 the estimates are 0.025(3) and 0.030(2), respectively. For weak correlations the fractal dimension returns to the uncorrelated value (91/48 in 2D; about 2.52295 in 3D). In 2D it rises as correlations strengthen, e.g. d_f=1.9128(5) at a=0.5 and 1.9602(8) at a=0.1, tending toward 2. The onset of the 2D change is not set simply by the extended Harris threshold. In 3D, estimates remain near the uncorrelated value for a≥1.5, but strong-correlation fits are unreliable at a≤1.
papers.methods_and_model: Numerical site percolation on periodic square and cubic lattices. Gaussian continuous site variables with covariance generated using a discrete Fourier-filtering method were thresholded into occupied/defect sites. The target covariance was C(r)=(1+r²)^(-a/2), with both Euclidean and Manhattan distance metrics tested. A global (ensemble-level) occupation-density mapping was used. A cluster was considered percolating when it wrapped across a specified lattice boundary. Threshold estimates came from finite-size extrapolation; cluster fractal dimensions were obtained by fitting the largest-cluster mass against lattice size. They generated 10^5 replicas per size: L=64–8192 in 2D and L=8–512 in 3D.
papers.relationship_to_projects: For a spatial percolation manuscript, this is a directly relevant benchmark if the manuscript treats lattice site percolation with power-law-correlated disorder: it supplies explicit square/cubic threshold estimates, fractal dimensions, and a clear warning that thresholds depend on metric and disorder construction. Comparisons should match the authors' global threshold mapping, periodic boundaries, wrapping definition, correlation function, and dimensionality; it is not a universal numeric benchmark outside that setup. For the one-orbital interface tight-binding notebook, relevance is only conceptual and indirect: the paper concerns classical geometric connectivity of occupied lattice sites, not a tight-binding Hamiltonian, interface states, orbital physics, conductance, or electronic localization, so it cannot validate those notebook results or provide direct numerical parameters.
papers.research_question: How do long-range power-law-correlated site defects affect percolation thresholds and the fractal dimension of critical largest clusters on square (2D) and cubic (3D) lattices? The authors also test sensitivity to the metric used to define correlation distances and whether changes in fractal dimension follow the extended Harris criterion.

synthesis.comparative_prospect: The spatial-correlation project has the more direct methodological bridge in the verified sources: three papers address long-range-correlated percolation, with finite-size methods, scaling ideas, and concrete cautions about model dependence. It also has a clear empirical motivation from reported film/sample heterogeneity, although no supplied study connects that heterogeneity to a measured nickelate percolation process. The interface-charge project has a strong conceptual foundation in oxide-interface electrostatics and bulk nickelate band-structure work, but the evidence is less directly matched to nickelate interfaces; model choices about charge bookkeeping, orbitals, and interface parameters require additional justification. Accordingly, spatial correlation appears more immediately benchmarkable against existing theory, while interface charge may have greater dependence on new system-specific derivation or validation. Neither prospect amounts to proof of novelty or validation, and the relative assessment is limited to these supplied verified records.
synthesis.interface_project_gap: The supplied record shows a gap between bulk nickelate parameterizations and interface-specific modeling. Botana–Norman, Nomura et al., and Lee–Pickett provide bulk electronic-structure or tight-binding context, including warnings about multiband pockets and orbital mixing, but no verified interface-specific one-orbital Hamiltonian, layer-dependent hopping/potential, or fitted interface charge term. The oxide-interface studies establish conceptual precedents for polarity, electronic reconstruction, and formal polarization, but concern other material systems and do not validate nickelate-specific orbital reduction or parameters. The interface-charge project therefore needs to state its charge convention and electrostatic boundary conditions explicitly and treat any single-orbital reduction as a scoped approximation pending nickelate-interface evidence. This is a bounded gap in the supplied verified set, not a universal novelty claim.
synthesis.literature_synthesis:
The verified literature separates into three evidence tiers. First, thin-film experiments establish superconductivity in several infinite-layer nickelates but do not resolve spatial connectivity or microscopic mechanism. Li et al. (2019, DOI 10.1038/s41586-019-1496-5) reported superconducting Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO2 with transition temperatures dependent on operational definition and sample-to-sample variation, including indications of lateral reduction inhomogeneity. Osada et al. (2020, DOI 10.1021/acs.nanolett.0c01392) reported superconducting Pr0.8Sr0.2NiO2 films, diamagnetic screening below the zero-resistance transition, and sample variability attributed to extended defects; neither study maps local superconducting domains or models percolation. Zeng et al. (2022, DOI 10.1126/sciadv.abl9927) found a Ca-doped La1−xCaxNiO2 superconducting dome and Hall-sign changes in much of the higher-doping range, while leaving the microscopic mechanism and multiband interpretation unresolved. These are material-specific motivation and empirical context, not direct tests of either proposed model.

Second, electronic-structure studies support the usefulness—but also the limits—of reduced nickelate Hamiltonians. Botana and Norman (2020, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevX.10.011024) calculated a d_x2−y2-derived single-band fit and compared it with a multiorbital picture that includes rare-earth-derived pockets and a larger charge-transfer energy than in CaCuO2. Nomura et al. (2019, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.100.205138) developed Wannier/cRPA-based multi- and single-orbital descriptions of bulk NdNiO2 and reported a single-orbital parameterization, but did not treat an interface or spatial percolation. Lee and Pickett (2004, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.70.165109) likewise supplied a bulk Ni x2−y2 band fit while emphasizing additional pockets and orbital mixing. These papers provide bulk reference points and cautions; their parameters do not independently establish a one-orbital interface model or its boundary terms.

Third, the correlated-disorder literature provides methodological precedent for the spatial project, with transferability limits. Weinrib and Halperin (1983, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.27.413) formulated an extended Harris criterion for power-law-correlated quenched disorder and discussed its application to percolation. Schrenk et al. (2013, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevE.88.052102) numerically studied two-dimensional triangular-lattice percolation with Fourier-filtered long-range-correlated disorder and Hurst-dependent scaling. Zierenberg et al. (2017, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevE.96.062125) studied square and cubic lattice site percolation, finding that thresholds depend on correlation construction and metric, while reporting fractal-dimension results with finite-size caveats. These works establish that correlation structure, lattice, and disorder-generation scheme matter; none studies superconducting nickelate films or validates a nickelate-specific spatial model.

Finally, oxide-interface papers motivate interface charge and electrostatic boundary conditions without validating nickelate parameters. Ohtomo and Hwang (2004, DOI 10.1038/nature02308) reported termination-dependent LAO/STO transport and high mobility for the conducting interface, but the full article was inaccessible in this verification. Okamoto and Millis (2004, DOI 10.1038/nature02450) reported theoretical electronic reconstruction at a Mott-insulator/band-insulator interface; details of the exact Nature paper are only partly accessible, and its companion PRB work is a distinct publication. Stengel and Vanderbilt (2009, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.80.241103) derived formal-polarization and displacement-field results for coherent insulating oxide interfaces. The latter two are useful conceptual precedents, but the model systems and assumptions differ from nickelates. Taken together, the verified sources support motivation and careful model construction, not a claim that either proposed nickelate model is already experimentally or theoretically validated.

synthesis.spatial_project_gap: The supplied record supports a clear model-specific gap: the verified nickelate experiments report transition and transport behavior, sample variation, extended defects, or possible reduction inhomogeneity, but none provides spatially resolved superconducting maps, cluster/connectivity statistics, or a percolation threshold. The verified long-range-correlated-percolation studies address classical lattice occupation models rather than superconducting nickelate films. Thus a spatial-correlation project could contribute by defining and testing a nickelate-relevant spatial model and observables, while distinguishing its disorder-generation assumptions and connectivity criteria from existing classical percolation results. This is a bounded gap in the supplied evidence, not a claim that no other relevant literature exists.
